core: The housekeeping department's role in cleanliness and room readiness
The cleaning workflow: room assignments, cleaning standards/SOPs, and inspection
Room status terminology (occupied, on-change/vacant-dirty, vacant-clean, vacant-ready, out-of-order) and its coordination with the front office via reports and the discrepancy report
PAR levels and linen/amenity inventory management
Productivity measures: rooms or credits per shift and minutes per room

Worker safety and ergonomics (Cal/OSHA Title 8 Section 3345 MIPP) as context for the labor-intensive nature of the work
Employment and wage scale of the occupation (BLS OEWS)

Whole-hotel organizational overview (owned by Hotel Operations)

General HR / employee-management theory (owned by Employee Management; labor is mentioned only as the main cost)

claims.claim: Housekeeping is the operational department responsible for the cleanliness, upkeep, and readiness of guest rooms and public areas, and for preparing (selling-ready) rooms that the front office then sells.
Labor is the largest single cost element of the housekeeping department, and housekeeping typically holds the largest workforce in a hotel; linen is commonly the department's second-largest expense.

Housekeeping and the front office must keep constant communication about room status; the front office informs housekeeping of check-outs, early arrivals, and late check-outs, and a housekeeping room status report is checked against front-office records so discrepancies can be identified and resolved.

Standard room status labels include OCC (occupied), VD/on-change (vacant and dirty, guest departed but room not yet cleaned), VC (vacant and clean), VR (vacant and ready for sale), and OOO (out of order); out-of-order rooms are not sellable and are deducted from the hotel's available inventory.

PAR stock is the minimum quantity of linen (and uniforms/supplies) needed to meet daily demand and keep operations running; hotels keep several par sets in circulation (for example one set on the beds/in rooms, one in the laundry, one in the floor linen closet, and one in the main linen room) so that clean stock is always available while soiled stock is being processed.

California Code of Regulations Title 8 Section 3345, the Hotel Housekeeping Musculoskeletal Injury Prevention Program, effective July 1, 2018, requires covered lodging employers to develop, implement, and maintain a written injury-prevention program with worksite evaluation, training, hazard correction, and annual review; there is no comparable federal OSHA ergonomics standard for the industry.

In May 2024 the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics counted roughly 1.52 million maids and housekeeping cleaners (SOC 37-2012) with a median annual wage of about $28,610, in an occupation requiring no formal educational credential and short-term on-the-job training.

Housekeeping productivity is managed with performance standards expressed as a time per room (minutes per room) or as rooms/credits per attendant per shift, and workload is balanced across attendants so each room receives enough time.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many par sets of linen a hotel should carry.
positions: Uttarakhand Open University's material describes a four-par circulation (one in use, one in the hotel laundry, one in the floor linen room, one in the main linen room).
Wider hospitality practice commonly teaches a range of about three to five par depending on laundry turnaround, property size, and whether an on-premise or outsourced laundry is used.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents par as a standard set as a management decision within a typical three-to-five-par range and uses a clearly hypothetical three-par figure in the worked example rather than asserting a single universal number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a specific square-footage cleaning cap exists in the Cal/OSHA hotel-housekeeping rule.
positions: Some secondary summaries reference a 5,000-square-feet-per-shift figure.
The text of CCR Title 8 Section 3345 as read on dir.ca.gov contains no such square-footage threshold.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The 5,000-square-feet figure is not asserted; the lesson describes Section 3345 only as a written injury-prevention-program mandate, which the regulation's own text supports.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft was treated as editorial intent only and not used as evidence; any of its specific wording or numbers were discarded unless independently verified here.
correctionsNeeded: Do not attribute a 5,000-square-feet cleaning cap to CCR Title 8 Section 3345; the regulation text does not contain it.
Present par levels as a management-set standard within a typical range, not a fixed universal count.
rightsIssues: All four substantive sources are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY; facts were synthesized and the prose written originally. No source wording was reproduced.

NCHM and Uttarakhand Open University materials carry no explicit open license, so they are used for facts only. U.S. BLS data and California regulatory text are public records but are likewise used as facts, not reproduced verbatim.

sourceRecords.provider: National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology (autonomous body under the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India)
sourceRecords.notes: Official Indian government hospitality-education textbook (First Edition 2024, ISBN 978-81-973763-2-0). Supports the department's role, room status terms (OCC, VC, VD, VR, OOO), housekeeping-front office coordination points and reports (arrival/departure lists, discrepancy report, room status report), linen room and laundry organization, and productivity/workload management. Retrieved as PDF via WebFetch and text-extracted locally with pypdf; used for facts only.

sourceRecords.title: Accommodation Management (HM-103), Self-Learning Material
sourceRecords.provider: Uttarakhand Open University, School of Management Studies
sourceRecords.notes: University open self-learning module. Supports labor as the largest cost element of housekeeping, housekeeping as the hotel's largest workforce, guest rooms as a majority of hotel sales, PAR stock definition and the four-par circulation example, linen exchange methods, and linen as the second-largest departmental expense. OCR quality is uneven, so used only for well-corroborated concepts, not exact wording. Retrieved as PDF via WebFetch and text-extracted locally with pypdf.

sourceRecords.title: California Code of Regulations, Title 8, Section 3345 - Hotel Housekeeping Musculoskeletal Injury Prevention Program
sourceRecords.notes: Primary regulatory text, read via WebFetch. Supports the effective date (July 1, 2018), the written-MIPP requirement, and its components (responsibility, worksite evaluation within three months and annually, hazard correction, training, annual effectiveness review). Confirmed the regulation contains no 5,000-square-feet cap. Used as context that hotel housekeeping is physically demanding and that this is a California, not federal, standard.

sourceRecords.title: Hotel Housekeeping Musculoskeletal Injury Prevention
sourceRecords.provider: State Compensation Insurance Fund of California (safeatworkca.com)
sourceRecords.notes: Secondary summary corroborating that Section 3345 was the first U.S. ergonomic standard written specifically for hotel housekeepers and that there is no national federal ergonomics standard. Used only to confirm the no-federal-standard framing; the regulatory facts themselves rest on the dir.ca.gov primary text.

sourceRecords.notes: Federal public-domain occupational data.
